title: It’s Not All About Crime: On the Need to Expand Criminology’s Life Course Lens
journal: Journal of Developmental and Life-Course Criminology
abstract: As criminologists, clearly crime is our core area of interest. Nevertheless, we may have focused too narrowly on this subject, both in constructing theories of onset and desistance, and in building programmatic efforts. I argue that criminal behavior and identities, and the crimes of associates should not be the only areas of concern for developing a comprehensive perspective on development and the life course. Thus, despite the real negative consequences of being labeled a delinquent or having a criminal record, identities are multidimensional and often relate to and are influenced by relationships with friends, romantic partners, and family members. In turn, attitudes and behaviors that relate to these important social realms are integral to the dynamics of “cognitive transformations,” the viability of “the good marriage effect,” and in relation to other processes that have been described in prior theorizing about criminal continuity and change. For example, infidelity is not a crime, but a recent longitudinal analysis documented a significant association between “cheating” on a partner and within-individual changes in self-reported criminal behavior. Widening the lens further, the recent focus on health and disability offers another promising direction for developing a more ‘full-bodied” approach to life course issues. The increased interest in strength based and holistic approaches to re-entry and other types of programs fit well with this broader life course perspective.
